title: AI Agents — Observability
description: Three instrumentation approaches (raw / LangChain4j / Spring AI) on one set of panels. CONVENTIONS: (1) every rate()/increase() query carries interval=1m — Micrometer PUSHES every 60 s and Grafana's default 15 s assumption makes $__rate_interval too narrow to hold two samples; (2) timeseries use palette-classic-by-name so a module keeps its colour on every panel — EXCEPT where the comparison is not between modules but between two sides of one thing, and then the colour encodes that instead (see 'MCP payload per call'); (3) grouping is by job (service.name), never by the framework tag — Spring AI series carry no framework label; (4) no query uses a *_max series — Micrometer puts max into the OTLP histogram point, but the collector-to-Prometheus path only materialises _sum, _count and _bucket; (5) EVERY panel answers for the selected time range — a number that ignores the range picker is a number nobody can trust, so cumulative counters are read with increase(), not max_over_time, except where a panel exists precisely to survive the blind spot below (Preflight 'reported LLM metrics'); (6) every bar gauge sets min 0 — with an auto minimum Grafana scales the bars to the DATA, so the smallest value always renders empty and the largest always renders full, which turns 1 and 2 into 'none' and 'max'. KNOWN BLIND SPOT: Micrometer creates counters lazily on first use, so the first push of a fresh process already carries a non-zero value and Prometheus never sees the series at 0 — rate()/increase() return 0 for a module's FIRST request after a restart. Send one warm-up request to every agent before a demo. THIS FILE IS THE DASHBOARD: it is provisioned from grafana/provisioning/dashboards and reloaded every 30 s, so edits made in the Grafana UI are overwritten on the next reload. Change the JSON, not the browser.

panels.title: Seconds since last metrics push, per module
panels.description: time() minus the timestamp of the newest JVM sample per job. Every module pushes on its own 60 s cycle (claude-mcp-server: 30 s), so values between 0 and ~60 s are normal and change on every refresh — they show where each process is in its cycle, not a problem. Green: pushed within the last 90 s. Red: the module is down, or it is up and its OTLP endpoint is wrong — both look identical from here, and both mean its panels will be empty. Expect 8 modules (9 with claude-mcp-server running under Claude Desktop). TWO ENTRIES FOR ONE MODULE ARE POSSIBLE: Claude Desktop can start claude-mcp-server more than once (two PIDs, one service.name), and both processes then push under the same job — which doubles every counter on this dashboard without any error anywhere.

panels.title: Modules pushing
panels.description: Distinct jobs with any JVM sample in the last 3 minutes. 8 = the reactor; 9 = plus claude-mcp-server.

panels.title: Modules that reported LLM metrics (range)
panels.description: Jobs for which gen_ai_client_token_usage_total has ANY sample inside the dashboard range. After a warm-up run of every agent this should read 7 (the two MCP servers have no model). This is the ONE panel that deliberately breaks the range-correlation rule in the dashboard description, and it is a presence check rather than a count: max_over_time asks 'did this module report at all', which stays true even for a module that made exactly one request since it started — increase() over a lazily created counter is 0 and would report that module as silent (exactly what showed 2 instead of 7 on 2026-09-02). A module that is UP (previous panel) but missing HERE after a request has a working JVM export and a broken GenAI listener — the failure that once hid the LangChain4j leg.

panels.title: LLM calls that failed (range)
panels.description: gen_ai_client_operation timer samples whose error tag is not 'none'. All three instrumentations tag it the same way — Spring AI through the Observation API, raw-agent and the LC4j listener by hand — so one query covers everything. 0 is the number you want to see before a demo; anything else means an OpenRouter/network problem that the happy path will not show you. Same first-sample blind spot as the token counters: a single failure right after a restart is invisible to increase().

panels.title: Tokens/min by module (input + output)
panels.description: Same numbers as the gen_ai.usage.* span attributes, aggregated. The 'total' token type is filtered out — it is input+output and only doubled the legend. Model is dropped from the grouping for the same reason; every module runs openai/gpt-4o-mini on the openrouter profile. A module's FIRST request after a restart does not show here (see the dashboard description) — send a warm-up request first.

panels.title: Tokens (dashboard range)
panels.description: Sums token usage over the CURRENT dashboard time range ($__range) — pick 'Last 15 minutes' and the numbers follow.

panels.title: Estimated cost (dashboard range)
panels.description: input tokens x $price_in + output tokens x $price_out, prices per 1M tokens from the dashboard variables at the top. The defaults are the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE for gpt-4o-mini — check the OpenRouter price page on the day and type the current numbers into the variables; nothing here is fetched. Four decimals because a single agent turn costs a fraction of a cent, and that IS the point of the panel. NOTE: this covers the CHAT leg only. multimodal-lab bills per picture, per character and per generated second, and two of its five capabilities never touch a ChatClient — see the mm_generation_* row.

panels.title: Estimated cost by module (dashboard range)
panels.description: Same formula as the stat, per job. This is the panel that answers 'which pattern is the expensive one' — orchestrator-workers on Spring AI runs a full model round per worker, chaining runs three, parallelization runs three at once; the bars make the difference visible without reading a trace. A module showing $0 after exactly one request since its restart is the first-sample blind spot, not a free call. min is pinned to 0 so the bars are proportional to the money, not to the spread between the cheapest and the most expensive module.

panels.title: LLM call duration — avg by module
panels.description: Source: gen_ai_client_operation_milliseconds sum/count, converted to seconds. raw-agent and LC4j emit the same meter name (gen.ai.client.operation) as Spring AI so all three land here. p95 lives in the next panel — 18 series on one chart was unreadable.

panels.title: LLM call duration — p95 by module
panels.description: histogram_quantile over the OTLP-exported buckets. With one or two calls per minute the p95 IS the slowest call, not a statistic — read it that way on stage. IF THIS PANEL IS EMPTY while avg (left) has data, the timers carry no _bucket series: check {__name__=~"gen_ai_client_operation_milliseconds.*"} in Prometheus. Buckets exist only when the timer publishes a percentile histogram; without them p95 cannot be computed from Prometheus and this panel should be dropped or the timers configured with publishPercentileHistogram().

panels.title: LLM calls/min by module
panels.description: One line per module. The shape tells the pattern before the trace does: chaining = 3 calls in a row, parallelization = 3 at once, orchestrator-workers = a burst of 10.

panels.title: Tool calls/min by module — all three frameworks
panels.description: Three meters, one panel. LangChain4j: gen_ai_client_tool_requests_total (tool calls the MODEL asked for, from the listener). Spring AI: spring_ai_tool_milliseconds_count (tool EXECUTIONS, from the spring.ai.tool observation). CONFIRMED 2026-09-02: this series appeared the moment the ChatClients were switched from ChatClient.builder(chatModel) — which hard-codes ObservationRegistry.NOOP — to the auto-configured ChatClient.Builder; the 'known Spring AI 2.0 gap' was that one call. raw-agent: not here yet — it has tool_call spans in Tempo but no counter; adding the same counter in RawAgentLoop is the missing 10 lines. The two meters count slightly different things (requested vs executed), which is itself worth a sentence on stage.

panels.title: Tool execution duration (Spring AI) — avg by tool
panels.description: Source: spring_ai_tool_milliseconds, tag spring_ai_tool_definition_name (confirmed in Prometheus 2026-09-02). Local tools (getSquad, getWeather) are sub-millisecond; getSecretRumors includes the human approval wait and dominates — it also has its own panel in the MCP row. MCP tools on the agent side (get_weather from spring-ai-agent-mcp) include the round-trip to mcp-server.

defaults.noValue: no Spring AI tool executions in range

panels.title: MCP tool calls/min by server & tool
panels.description: Hand-written meters: McpToolTelemetry (common, used by mcp-server) and CodeToolsService (claude-mcp-server) emit the same names and tags. Spring AI 2.0 instruments tool calling on the AGENT side only, so without these wrappers the server side of a propagated trace is a bare `http post /mcp`.

panels.title: MCP tool duration by server & tool (avg)
panels.description: Micrometer OTLP exports timers in milliseconds, converted to seconds here. Approval-gated tools are EXCLUDED from this panel on purpose — they are human time, not machine time, and have their own panel to the right.

panels.title: Human-in-the-loop wait — gated tool duration (avg)
panels.description: The tools that block until a person decides: save_note and delete_note on mcp-server (mcp_tool_duration), and getSecretRumors in patterns-spring-ai (spring_ai_tool, agent side). This is the one latency in the whole system that no model or network explains — it is how long the person at /approvals took. Computed as sum/count per rate window; gated calls are rare, so within a window this is normally the duration of THE one call, not an average that dilutes it. An earlier version read the timer's _max gauge and stayed empty: Micrometer sends max inside the OTLP histogram point, but the collector-to-Prometheus path does not materialise a _max series. patterns-langchain4j is missing here by construction: its getSecretRumors has a tool_call SPAN (Tempo) but no timer.

panels.title: MCP payload per call (avg chars, request vs response)
panels.description:
CHARACTERS, NOT TOKENS. An MCP server never sees token counts — no model, no tokenizer, and MCP reports no usage back — so the length of the strings exchanged is the only honest measure (roughly 3-4 chars per token for code, as an order of magnitude). Split by direction because the two are wildly asymmetric per tool: MEASURED 2026-09-27, read_file sends 48 chars and returns 24 700 — a factor of 500, and write_file is the exact mirror image (36 K in, 78 out). Measuring only the response would make write_file look free.

COLOUR ENCODES DIRECTION, NOT SERIES NAME — the one panel on this dashboard that breaks the palette-classic-by-name convention. With colour by name, 'write_file request' (36.5 K) and 'read_file response' (35.2 K) drew as two near-identical pink bars of near-identical height, which is the worst possible outcome for a panel whose entire point is that those two numbers belong to OPPOSITE directions. Orange is into the server, blue is out of it; tool names live in the legend table and the tooltip, where a name belongs.

Source: mcp_tool_payload_size_chars_{sum,count}. Resources and prompts are deliberately NOT on this panel — they are picked by hand a few times an hour, so their rate() series sat at zero between the spikes and added six flat lines for nothing; they have their own two panels below.

targets.expr: sum by (job, tool, direction) (rate(mcp_tool_payload_size_chars_sum[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (job, tool, direction) (rate(mcp_tool_payload_size_chars_count[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Failed MCP tool calls (range)
panels.description: outcome is derived from the 'ERROR:' prefix of the returned text, NOT from thrown exceptions — these servers answer the model with error strings so nothing propagates. Empty panel = no failures.

panels.title: MCP resources & prompts
panels.description:
A DELIBERATELY UNUSUAL METRIC: it measures neither latency nor errors, because neither is interesting here — reading a resource is a file read and rendering a prompt is a string concatenation, both over in milliseconds. It answers the one question nothing else in the stack can: WAS THIS PICKED, AND HOW OFTEN? A prompt nobody chooses is a dead menu entry plus a maintenance obligation, and without this bar the only evidence would be asking people. Source: mcp_primitive_calls_total from McpPrimitiveTelemetry (claude-mcp-server), tagged primitive=resource|prompt|completion.

min IS PINNED TO 0. Without it Grafana scales bars to the data, so the smallest value renders as an empty bar and the largest as a full one — with counts of 1 and 2 that reads as 'never used' and 'used constantly', which is a lie about a one-call difference. Pinned to 0, a bar is proportional to the count.

FOLLOWS THE TIME RANGE, like every other counter on this dashboard. An earlier version used max_over_time and reported the running total since the server started — which never changed when you moved the range picker, and a number that ignores the range is a number nobody can trust. The price of increase() is the blind spot in the dashboard description: the FIRST call of a freshly started server is invisible, because Micrometer creates the counter lazily and Prometheus never sees it at zero. Use a resource twice after a restart, or widen the range past the restart, and the count is exact.

NOTE ON completion: the methods exist and register, but Claude Desktop never calls completion/complete — verified in the client protocol log, where the handshake asks only for tools/list, prompts/list and resources/list. A server can expose a capability no client asks for, which is the mirror image of mcp-server advertising resources and prompts while registering none.

panels.title: MCP resources & prompts in time
panels.description:
The companion of the bar gauge above: that one answers HOW MANY in the range, this one answers WHEN inside it. Together they are the whole story of a primitive nobody can otherwise observe — the client renders these in a menu and this server never learns what the human did next.

Styled and queried exactly like 'MCP tool calls/min by server & tool' — same meter shape, same rate()x60 per minute, same line style — so the two read the same way and can sit in one row without a mental gear change. Colour stays by series name here, unlike the payload panel: these series have no two sides to distinguish, only six different things.

WITH A HANDFUL OF PICKS PER HOUR THE VALUES ARE FRACTIONS: one call inside a one-minute rate window is 1/min, one call seen across a three-minute window is 0.33/min. That is the same arithmetic as the tool panel above, where a single read_file also shows as 0.3 — read the spikes as 'something happened here', not as a throughput.

AN EMPTY PANEL IS USUALLY TRUE: it means nothing was picked in the selected range. Check the bar gauge above before assuming the metric is broken — if it is also empty at a wide range, the server has not served a resource or a prompt at all.

panels.title: Traces — click a trace ID to open the waterfall
Latest agent requests (Tempo)
panels.description: TraceQL search on the span NAME, which Spring Boot 4 sets to 'http <method> <route>' for every server span. WHY A TABLE: Grafana's 'Traces' panel renders ONE trace (a waterfall for a trace-ID query) and answers a TraceQL search result — which is a list — with 'No data found in response'. A search result is a table; the Tempo datasource attaches a link to the trace ID column that opens the waterfall in Explore. If the list is empty right after a request, Tempo's ingester needs a few seconds (same lag as 'Logs for this span'). This query matches HTTP server spans only, so the STDIO server's mcp_tool / mcp_resource / mcp_prompt spans are not listed here — find them in Explore with {resource.service.name="claude-mcp-server"}.

panels.title: Requests/min by service & endpoint
panels.description: Actuator endpoints are excluded at the source by the shared ObservationPredicate (module: common). /approvals polling from the chat-ui is NOT excluded — that flat line on the patterns modules is the UI asking for pending approvals.

panels.title: HTTP 4xx/5xx per min
panels.description: Flat zero = zero errors (the query filters status 4xx/5xx). A 500 on /api/v1/patterns/parallel from 2026-09-02 was the Jackson 3 FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES change — fixed in ParallelizationPattern.

panels.title: Heap used by service
panels.description: Gauges — no rate(), so these render at any range. That asymmetry is the tell when the panels above go blank: gauges fine + rate panels empty = window narrower than the push interval, not missing metrics.

panels.title: Live threads by service
panels.description: Watch mcp-server during a pending approval — virtual threads keep this flat while a request blocks.
